steps.title: Why start with Orders?
steps.change: FROM Orders supplies one row per purchase because the report counts order IDs and amounts. Orders 17–21 still count despite NULL amounts, and a purchase with a missing customer must remain.
steps.added_sql: SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Total_Order_Amount FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderID;
steps.sql: SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Total_Order_Amount FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderID;

steps.title: Why LEFT JOIN Customers?
steps.change: Orders already carries the buyer key. The LEFT JOIN matches order 12 to customer 3 in Maharashtra and keeps order 11 with its buyer ID 99 and a NULL customer match. All 49 orders survive.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID AS ordered_by, o.Total_Order_Amount,
       c.CustomerID AS matched_customer, c.State
FROM Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
ORDER BY o.OrderID;
steps.sql:
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID AS ordered_by, o.Total_Order_Amount,
       c.CustomerID AS matched_customer, c.State
FROM Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
ORDER BY o.OrderID;

steps.title: Why label the state before GROUP BY?
steps.change: Order 11 has no matched customer. Orders 22–26 match customer 4, whose state is NULL. Both receive Unknown, the same label already stored for customer 5 on orders 27–30.
steps.added_sql: SELECT Orders.OrderID, Orders.CustomerID, COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, Orders.Total_Order_Amount FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID ORDER BY Orders.OrderID;
steps.sql: SELECT Orders.OrderID, Orders.CustomerID, COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, Orders.Total_Order_Amount FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID ORDER BY Orders.OrderID;

steps.title: Why group by the displayed state?
steps.change: The 49 order rows form five state groups. Unknown collects orders 11 and 22–30. Goa has nine orders. Each other state group has ten.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, COUNT(*) AS group_rows FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
GROUP BY COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown');
steps.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, COUNT(*) AS group_rows FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
GROUP BY COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown');

steps.title: Why count buyers and orders separately?
steps.change: In Unknown, buyer IDs 99, 4 and 5 contribute 1 + 5 + 4 orders. That gives three distinct buyers and ten orders. Maharashtra has ten orders from buyer 3 alone.
steps.added_sql: SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, COUNT(DISTINCT Orders.CustomerID) AS customers, COUNT(Orders.OrderID) AS orders FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
steps.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state, COUNT(DISTINCT Orders.CustomerID) AS customers, COUNT(Orders.OrderID) AS orders FROM Orders LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
GROUP BY COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown');

steps.title: Why do SUM and AVG read only known amounts?
steps.change: Maharashtra has five amounts of 200 and five NULLs. SUM gives 1000 and AVG uses the five known amounts, giving 200. Karnataka also totals 1000 but averages 100 across ten amounts. All ten Kerala amounts are NULL, so both metrics are NULL.
steps.added_sql:
SELECT
    COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state,
    COUNT(DISTINCT Orders.CustomerID) AS customers,
    COUNT(Orders.OrderID) AS orders,
    SUM(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS order_value,
    AVG(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS avg_order_value
FROM Orders
LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
steps.sql:
SELECT
    COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state,
    COUNT(DISTINCT Orders.CustomerID) AS customers,
    COUNT(Orders.OrderID) AS orders,
    SUM(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS order_value,
    AVG(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS avg_order_value
FROM Orders
LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
GROUP BY COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown');

steps.title: Why use HAVING for the 10-order minimum?
steps.change: Goa has nine orders and drops out. The four ten-order groups survive, including Kerala because eligibility counts order IDs even when amounts are missing.
steps.sql:
SELECT
    COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown') AS state,
    COUNT(DISTINCT Orders.CustomerID) AS customers,
    COUNT(Orders.OrderID) AS orders,
    SUM(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS order_value,
    AVG(Orders.Total_Order_Amount) AS avg_order_value
FROM Orders
LEFT JOIN Customers ON Customers.CustomerID = Orders.CustomerID
GROUP BY COALESCE(NULLIF(TRIM(Customers.State), ''), 'Unknown')
HAVING COUNT(Orders.OrderID) >= 10;

steps.title: Why sort by average order value?
steps.change: The four surviving rows are ordered by average amount: Maharashtra (200), Karnataka (100), Unknown (50), then Kerala (NULL). Together they account for 40 orders.
